full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J.: These two appeals under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, one at the instance of accused Md. Dulal Mia being Criminal Appeal No. 605 of 1989 and the other at the instance of accused Siraj Mia being Criminal Appeal No. 266 of 1990 are directed against two orders dated 12.11.89 and 2.4.1990 respectively passed by the Special Tribunal for Prevention of Smuggling, Sylhet in Special Tribunal Case No. 107 of 1988 rejecting the prayers for bail of the accused-appellants. The appeals being of the same nature and having arisen out of the same case are heard together and disposed of by the following judgment. 

 2. The appellants along with 3 others are accused in the above case under section 25B of the Special Powers Act. The facts of the case as alleged in the First Information Report arc that on 26.1.1987 at night the informant Md. Nurul Islam, Sub-Inspector of Police, Kotwali Police Station, Sylhet was on a patrol duty in Sylhet town and at about 4-30 AM he received a secret information that in Laldighirpar Hawker's market a man was loading some old clothes (garments) in a truck to go to India through Tamabil Road and to smuggle out the same. On receipt of that news, he along with some other police personnel lay in ambush in Supari Ghat, Sylhet, At about 5-00 PM he found that the loaded truck was accordingly running. When the same came near he asked the truck-driver to stop by giving signal but the truck-driver without paying any heed to the signal went on running away. Then the truck was followed by the informant by a patrol car and after crossing the Pargan Bazar he was able to compel the truck-driver to stop the truck. The truck driver accused Md. Dulal Mia and the helper accused Siraj Mia tried to escape when they were caught, but the owner of the goods accused Shamsul Huq alias Disco and another accused Tafazzal succeeded to run away The truck was full of old garments worth Tk. 100000.00 which were seized in presence of local witnesses and a seizure-list was prepared and then the case was started by filing a First Information Report under section 156(8) of the Customs Act read with section 25B of the Special Powers Act of 1974. On registration of the case, the informant himself took up the investigation and after completion of the same submitted charge-sheet on 13.2.1988 against the accused appellants and 3 others as stated above. 

 3. On receipt of the charge-sheet, the learned Upazila Magistrate, Sylhet sent the case-records to the learned Special Tribunal, Sylhet who after taking cognizance of the case under section 25B of the Special Powers Act on 26.6.1988 sent the same to the Court of Mr. Rinoy Kumar Bose, the Special Tribunal for prevention of smuggling, Sylhet for trial. The Special Tribunal received the case records on 30.6.88 and at that time these two appellants Md. Dulal Mia and Siraj Mia were on bail earlier granted by the learned Upazila Magistrate. Accused Shamsul Hoque alias Disco, of course, was in custody and the 2 other accused namely Manik Mia and Tafazzal Ali were absconding. 

 4. It appears from the order-sheet of the case that these appellants surrendered before the Special Tribunal and prayed for bail but their prayer for bail was rejected and they were sent to jail hajat by an order dated 12.7.88 and since then they are in jail custody. Subsequently co-accused Manik Mia surrendered before the Tribunal and filed an application for bail on the ground of illness. The Special Tribunal on consideration of the same granted him an ad-inter in bail on 29.8.88 and the same was ultimately confirmed having no objection from the Public Prosecutor on 25.9.88 and he is still continuing on the same bail. So far accused Shamsul Hoque alias Disco is concerned who alleged to be the owner of the seized goods on his failure to obtain bail from the Special Tribunal, moved this Court and succeeded to obtain a Rule in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 242 of 1989 which was made absolute after hearing both the sides by a Division Bench of this Court on 20.8.1989 and he was enlarged on bail to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. He is still continuing on the same bail granted by this Court. So far accused Tofazzal is concerned he is still absconding. It appears from the records that warrant of arrest was issued against him by the Special Tribunal since 30.6.88, but no Return of Execution of the Warrant of Arrest has been received by the trial Court as yet. Meanwhile these two accused-appellants filed applications before the Special Tribunal praying for bail on different occasions but their prayers for bail were rejected mainly on the ground that the police found a prima facie case against them. Lastly, their applications for bail were rejected by the Special Tribunal on 12.11.89 and 2.4.1990 respectively. Being aggrieved by the said order dated 12.11.89 of the Special Tribunal, the appellant Md. Dulal Mia preferred Criminal Appeal No. 605 of 1989 in this Court which was admitted for hearing on 17.1.1990. Subsequently appellant Siraj Mia being aggrieved by the order of the learned Special Tribunal dated 2.4.1990 preferred Criminal Appeal No. 266 of 1990 in this Court which was also admitted for hearing and there was an order for analogous hearing of the above two appeals and accordingly they are taken up for analogous hearing. 

 (i) That the appellants are innocent driver and helper of the seized truck and they had no connection with the smuggling of the alleged goods and as such there is no prima facie case against them and they are entitled to bail. 

 (iii) That the appellants have been held in jail custody since 12.7.1988 for about 2½ years without trial and this is highly derogatory to the principles of criminal justice and the fundamental rights as guaranteed and enshirned under Article 35(3) of our Constitution i.e the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and further there is no immediate prospect of the trial of the case and as such the appellants should be enlarged on bail in the interest of justice due to inordinate and unreasonable delay in the trial. 

 6. Now, let us consider the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants one after another. In reply to the 1st submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants, it is submitted by the learned Advocate for the State that section 32 of the Special Powers Act is a bar in granting bail to the accused appellants. He further submits that it cannot be said that there is no prima facie case against the appellants or that they are innocent when after investigation the police has found prima facie case against them and the court has taken cognizance of the same under section 25B of the Special Powers Act. He refers us to the First Information Report and the charge-sheet in this case and submits that the accused appellants in spite of the signal by the police did not stop their running truck and ultimately they were caught red-handed after a chase. The learned Advocate for the State, however, opposes the prayer for bail. 

 7. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates on the first point and we are of the view that the submissions relate to the merit of the case which can be decided only on evidence at the trial and we should not express any definite opinion on the same at this stage lest it prejudices the parties. So far the bar of section 32 of the Special Powers Act, we have held earlier in a case that the bar is not absolute. It depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. 

 8. Now, with regard to the 2nd point urged before us regarding the alleged discrimination in granting bail to some co-accused of the case, let us see how far it is correct. It is not disputed that one co-accused Manik Mia has been granted bail by the trial Court and another co-accused Shamsul Hoque alias Disco has been granted bail by this Court. The allegations as brought in the First Information Report and the charge sheet are to the effect that these appellants, one being the driver of the truck and the other being the helper were caught red-handed with the alleged goods and the alleged owner of the seized goods accused Shamsul Hoque alias Disco managed to flee away along with some other co-accused. The learned Advocate for the appellants, however, submits that whatever may be the allegations in the First Information Report the charge-sheet was submitted against all 5 accused persons and cognizance was taken by the learned Special Tribunal on submission of the charge-sheet under section 25B of the Special Powers Act against all of them. So, they are all on the same footing and there should not be any discrimination in granting bail to some of the accused and refusing the same to the rest. He has relied on some decisions in this regard reported in 35 DLR (AD) 279, 1983 BCR (AD) 170 and 42 DLR (AD) 52. The principles as laid down in the above decisions are not disputed. Now, question is how far these are applicable in the facts and circumstances of this case. In the instant case these appellants were running truck from which the alleged smuggled goods were seized and they were caught-red handed and whereas co-accused Manik Mia who is on bail granted by the trial Court was not named in the First Information Report and he was granted bail on the ground of his illness. Co-accused Shamsul Hoque alias Disco who is alleged to be the owner of the alleged smuggled goods has been granted bail by this Court on an observation to the effect. 

 10. Now, let us consider the last submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants about the alleged inordinate and unusual delay in holding the trial. We have gone through the order-sheet of the case and we find that the appellants are in jail custody since 12.7.88 for about 2½ years without trial. The case was received by the Special Tribunal on 26.6.88 and the same was transferred to the present Special Tribunal for prevention of smuggling, Sylhet for trial on 30.6.88. It appears that one of the co-accused Tofazzal Ali has been in abscondence from the very beginning and the order-sheet further shows that at different times only Warrant of Arrest was issued by the Court against the said accused Tofazzal Ali but no SR of the same was received by the Court and this way quite a long period elapsed and no positive step was taken by the prosecution or the Court to make the case ready for hearing either by splitting up the case of the absconding accused under section 512 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or by following the provisions of section 339 B(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as amended and issuing gazette notification and publishing the same in the newspapers also for trial of the accused in absentia. It appears further from the order-sheet that there was also prayer by the accused for holding early trial of the case. So far, the application of the provisions of Ordinance 24 of 1982 i.e. the Criminal Procedure Code (2nd Amendment) Ordinance regarding speedy and absentia trial, in a case under the Special Powers Act, the learned Advocate for the appellant has referred to a decision reported in 10 BLD (AD) 190 which shows that the provisions of the said amendment of the Cr PC are very much applicable in the trial of a case under the Special Powers Act The learned Advocate appearing for the State, on persusal of the order-sheet and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, however, concedes that there has been unreasonable and inordinate delay in holding the trial in this case and no tangible and proper step appears to have been taken either by the prosecution or by the Court to hold the trial in due course. The speedy and public trial is a fundamental right guaranteed by our Constitution in Article 35(3) of the same which reads as follows: 

 But, unfortunately, in many a case, we find dereliction and also denial of the said right which cannot but be deprecated. It may be noticed that towards the fulfillment of this Constitutional provision, CrPC was amended fixing time limit for disposal of cases and also it appears that by amendment of section 27 of the Special Powers Act by Ordinance 40/77, the following provision was incorporated as under. 

 Unfortunately, in the instant case, the Special Tribunal has not taken any proper step towards this direction for holding trial of the case and consequently these appellants have been languishing in jail hajat without trial for about 2-1/2 years. The learned Advocate for the State also found it difficult to explain the unusual and unreasonable delay for holding trial of the instant case under the Special Powers Act. Mr. MA Matin the learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the privilege of bail should not be withheld by way of punishment. He submits that this long detention of the appellants in jail hajat without satisfactory explanation amounts to a deprivation of the privilege of bail to the appellants by way of punishment and as such they should no longer be kept in custody without trial and be enlarged on bail in the interest of justice. In support of his contention he has relied on some decisions reported in 1983 BCR(AD) 50 and 42 DLR (AD) 394. The learned Advocate further submits that inordinate and unreasonable delay in the trial has been found to be a good ground for enlarging the accused on bail even in a case of murder and the same principle equally applies in a case under the Special Powers Act. In this regard the learned Advocate for the appellants has referred to a number of decisions reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 21, 20 DLR (SC) 339 and 42 DLR (AD) 8. 

 11. We have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants and have noticed the principles as laid down in the above decisions cited before us and we are of the view that there is much force in the last contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants regarding bail on the ground of unreasonable or inordinate delay in the trial of the case and the appellants ought to have been granted bail at least till the actual trial starts. 

 12. Having regard to our above discussion and the facts and circumstances of the case, we are inclined to set aside the impugned orders of the learned Special Tribunal and to enlarge the appellants on bail till disposal of the case. 

 13. In the result, the appeals arc allowed. The impugned orders arc set aside and we hereby allow the appellants Md. Dulal Mia and Siraj Mia to be released on bail to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet till disposal of the case. 

 We also direct expeditious trial of the case. 

 Let the records of the case be sent down at once.
